doc.title: Bill Dobbins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

chapter: Kent State and the Eastman job
title: Festivals, Cleveland piano job and the Eddie's band's Montreux trip
summary: The Kent band reached national festivals, Dobbins played six nights a week in Cleveland (1971-73), and the Eddie's band was funded to go to Montreux in 1969.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: So I kept in touch with Clark over the years and they had these competitive festivals in those days that were sponsored by DownBeat magazine and some of the tobacco or liquor companies. They had regional festivals. And the amazing thing was that the winners in different categories, like big band, small group, soloist, composer/arranger, and so on, of these regional festivals. And they had all their expenses paid to go to a national festival. And we were a national finalist two or three years before I moved on from the Kent scene. And a couple of those years Clark was one of the judges, so we would see Clark again from time to time in our different activities as a band, and he was always very encouraging and helpful and friendly. And after I graduated from Kent with a bachelor’s in classical piano and composition, a master’s in composition, we moved to Cleveland in the summer of 1971. There was a great position there for a musician. There had been an entertainment show that originated from Cleveland through the sixties, by an entertainer- singer named Mike Douglas, “The Mike Douglas Show.” And when the show moved to Philadelphia, the band leader for the show was a female pianist named Ellie Frankel. And when the show moved to Philadelphia they took her but she had to hire Philadelphia musicians. So the drummer from the Cleveland band, he took over this gig that she had, it was a six-night-a-week gig at this great restaurant and bar in downtown Cleveland, not far from the stadium called The Theatrical Restaurant. And the pianist that had been doing this, after she had left for a number of years, decided that he didn’t want to do it anymore, so I ended up playing jazz six nights a week and getting paid pretty decent money for it, so we lived there from ’71 to ’73. And while we were at Kent there was a music critic that wrote for the Akron Beacon Journal named Ted Price. And he was a big fan of the big band at Kent State. In fact in 1969 in the little town of Kent — I think there are about 45 thousand people in the town and more than 20 thousand at the university — they have this little strip there. There was a restaurant/bar called Eddie’s. And we convinced the guy that ran Eddie’s to let the big band play there on Monday nights. And we made scale — 15 dollars a person. He charged a buck or two at the door, and between that and the meals and bar he made out okay. So we played there every Monday night for

a couple of years. And in ’69 we got an invitation to play at the Montreux Jazz Festival in Switzerland. And the music school wouldn’t help us at all as far as raising money, you know, they weren’t interested in that at all. So the people that came to hear us down at Eddie’s, they found out about this, and they were so incensed by it that a bunch of the businessmen who came down to hear the band, they organized a whole series of fundraising concerts, and raised all the money to send the band to Switzerland. It’s like something that you wouldn’t even believe would have happened. So Ted was also definitely a part of that. For some reason at one point this job opening came up with the Buffalo papers, and he moved from Akron to Buffalo. And of course it’s just an hour or so from Eastman, so he used to come here and hear concerts from time to time. He really fell in love with the Eastman Jazz Ensemble.
